### Hiring for a job that runs a million times

You are hiring someone to answer one question, over and over, a million times a month.

You could hire a professor. Brilliant, expensive, occasionally slow, and enormously
over-qualified for "is this email spam?". You could hire a bright graduate: fast, cheap, right
most of the time, out of their depth on the hard 5%. Or you could hire the professor *for the hard
ones only* and let the graduate handle the rest.

Nobody would hire the professor for everything and then complain about the salary bill. Yet that
is exactly what most teams do with models, and it is why their first invoice is a shock.

### The triangle you cannot escape

Every model choice trades between three things, and you may have any two:

- **Quality** — how often the answer is right, on *your* task.
- **Cost** — money per answered request.
- **Speed** — how long the user waits.

A bigger model is usually better and always slower and dearer. A smaller one is faster and
cheaper and gives up something. What makes this bearable is that the trade is *per task*: the
model that is overkill for classifying an email may be exactly right for drafting the reply.
Which is why serious systems use **more than one model** and route between them (Week 34 M3).

### Hosted, or your own?

Two ways to get a model, and the difference is not really technical.

**Hosted (an API).** Someone else runs it. You send text, you get text, you pay per tile. Nothing
to operate, the newest models arrive without you doing anything, and your costs scale with usage —
which is wonderful at low volume and eye-watering at high volume.

**Open-weight (your own).** The model's numbers are published; you run it on hardware you rent or
own (Week 26 M5). You pay for the machine, not the tile — so the cost per request falls as usage
rises. In exchange you inherit an operational job: capacity, upgrades, on-call.

The honest summary, before the arithmetic in Layer 2: **hosted models win until your volume is
large and your task is narrow.** Most teams should start hosted and stay there longer than pride
suggests.

### The number that actually decides

Not the benchmark. Your task.

Public leaderboards measure general ability on general questions. You have a *specific* job —
classifying your tickets, summarising your documents, answering about your product — and models
that rank identically on a leaderboard routinely differ by a wide margin on one particular narrow
task. The only measurement that counts is the one you run on your own examples.

Which gives you a procedure rather than an opinion, and it takes an afternoon:

1. Take **twenty real inputs** from your product, with the answers you would accept (this is Week
   31's eval set — you will need it anyway).
2. Run **three or four candidate models** on all twenty, with the same prompt.
3. Record for each: how many you would ship unedited, the cost of the twenty, and the p95 latency.
4. Pick the cheapest model that clears your quality bar — not the best one.

That last line is the whole discipline. The goal is not the best model; it is the *cheapest model
that is good enough*, because the difference is pure margin on every request you will ever serve.

<Check>
**The answer to the opening question, plainly.** You choose by **running your own twenty examples
through three or four candidates and picking the cheapest one that clears your bar** — not by
reading a leaderboard, because general rankings and your narrow task frequently disagree. Behind
that sits a trade you cannot escape between quality, cost and speed, which is why real systems
route easy work to small models and reserve the expensive one for the hard cases. Hosted models
win until your volume is large and your task is stable; then owning the machine starts to pay.
</Check>

<Accordion title="Checkpoint — 5 questions before you continue">
1. **What three things trade against each other in every model choice?** Quality, cost and speed.
2. **Why is a leaderboard a weak basis for a decision?** It measures general ability; your task is narrow, and rankings often disagree at that level.
3. **What is the goal when choosing?** The cheapest model that clears your quality bar — not the best model.
4. **When does running your own model start to make sense?** High, steady volume on a stable task, where cost per machine-hour beats cost per tile — and you can carry the operational job.
5. **Why do serious systems use more than one model?** Because the right choice differs per task; easy work is routed to a small model and only hard cases reach the expensive one.
</Accordion>

### The question this page leaves open

You have chosen a model. It is somebody else's, running on somebody else's hardware, billed per
tile — and if it is an open-weight one, it is 16 GB of numbers that will not fit on the card you
own.

Which is the same problem from two directions: to bring a model home, it has to get smaller.
That is [Module 1 — Numeric precision & quantization](/curriculum/p4/week-26/1-numeric-precision-quantization).
  </Tab>

  <Tab title="🔵 Layer 2 — Build">
    **You ship code for a living?** This layer is yours — trade-offs, real tools, real versions.

    "Which model should we use?" arrives in your first week and again every quarter. Answering it
    with evidence rather than preference is a small, repeatable piece of engineering.

### The bake-off in practice

```python
# bakeoff.py — same prompt, same inputs, several models
import time, statistics

CANDIDATES = ["claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", "claude-sonnet-5", "claude-opus-5"]

def evaluate(call, model, cases, prompt_builder):
    ok, tiles, lat = 0, 0, []
    for inp, expected in cases:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        out, usage = call(model, *prompt_builder(inp))
        lat.append(time.monotonic() - t0)
        tiles += usage.input_tokens + usage.output_tokens
        ok += int(accept(out, expected))          # your own acceptance check
    return {
        "model": model,
        "quality": ok / len(cases),
        "tiles": tiles,
        "p95_s": round(statistics.quantiles(lat, n=20)[18], 2),
    }
```

Report it as a table and let it decide. The rule that survives review: **cheapest model above the
bar**, with the bar written down before you ran anything.

### What the sticker price leaves out

Per-tile pricing is the smallest part of the real number. Also count:

- **Prompt overhead.** Your system prompt and examples are re-sent on every request. A long prompt
  on a cheap model can cost more than a short prompt on an expensive one.
- **Output length.** Output tiles typically cost several times input tiles; a model that answers
  in three paragraphs where another answers in one is not the cheaper model.
- **Retries.** A model that fails your format check 5% of the time costs 105% of its list price,
  plus the latency of the retry.
- **Thinking tiles.** Reasoning models bill for work you never see (Week 25 M6).

Compute **cost per *accepted* answer**, not cost per call. It reorders the table more often than
not.

### The switching cost nobody budgets

Prompts are not portable (Week 25 M0). Changing model means re-running your eval set, re-tuning
prompts, possibly re-doing few-shot examples, and re-checking every structured-output path. Budget
a few days, not an afternoon — and design for it: keep the model name in configuration, keep
prompts in files, and keep the eval set current. Those three habits turn a migration from a
project into a Tuesday.

    Model choice is not a decision you make once. It is a decision you re-make every few months,
    whether you want to or not.

### Deprecation is a certainty, not a risk

Hosted models are retired on a schedule that is not yours (Week 34 M5). Plan for it structurally:
pin an exact model version in configuration rather than an alias, keep the eval set runnable on
demand, and treat "re-qualify on the successor" as routine maintenance with a calendar entry —
not an incident.

Open weights invert this: nobody can take the model away, and nobody will improve it for you
either. You have traded a deprecation risk for a stagnation risk.

### Routing and cascades

Two patterns worth knowing once your volume is real:

- **Routing.** A cheap classifier decides which model handles each request. Effective when the
  hard cases are recognisable *before* answering.
- **Cascade.** Try the small model first; if a confidence check or validator fails, escalate to the
  larger one. Effective when hard cases are only recognisable *after* an attempt — and the
  arithmetic works whenever the small model succeeds often enough to pay for the occasional double
  call.

Both are cost engineering (Week 34 M3), and both add a failure mode: the router itself can be
wrong, so measure end-to-end quality, never just the router's accuracy.

### What changes when a new model lands

Do not upgrade on the announcement. Run the eval set, compare cost per accepted answer, and check
the things that quietly change between versions: default verbosity, instruction-following
strength, structured-output reliability, and tool-calling behaviour. Then canary it (Week 34 M5).
A better model that is more verbose can raise your bill while raising your quality — you should
know which trade you just made.

## Hands-on

Run the bake-off on a real task of yours with three models and twenty inputs. Produce the table:
quality, cost per accepted answer, p95 latency. Then write one sentence naming the model you chose
and why. That sentence is what a design review actually wants.

## Apply it at work

**For the student.** "I benchmarked three models on twenty real cases and chose the cheapest that
cleared the bar" is a stronger portfolio sentence than any model name.

**For the professional.** Put the model name in configuration today, if it is not already. It is
ten minutes now and saves a week when the deprecation email arrives.

## Assessment

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="5 concept questions">
  1. Name the three-way trade in model choice. (Quality, cost, speed.)
  2. Why is cost per call misleading? (Prompt overhead, output length, retries and hidden thinking tiles — measure cost per *accepted* answer.)
  3. When does self-hosting start to win? (High steady volume on a stable task, where per-hour beats per-tile and you can carry the operations.)
  4. What is the difference between routing and a cascade? (Routing decides before answering; a cascade escalates after a failed attempt.)
  5. Why pin an exact model version? (Aliases move under you; deprecations and silent upgrades change behaviour you have evaluated.)
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Coding challenge">
  Write `bakeoff(models, cases, prompt_builder, accept)` that returns a table of quality, total
  tiles, cost per accepted answer and p95 latency, and prints the cheapest model clearing a given
  bar. Hidden tests check: a model that fails every case is never selected; ties break toward the
  cheaper model; and the cost calculation counts input and output tiles at different rates.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Interview questions (junior / mid / senior)">
  - **Junior:** "How would you decide which model to use for a new feature?"
  - **Mid:** "Our costs tripled after a model upgrade that also improved quality. How do you decide whether to keep it?"
  - **Senior:** "Design a model strategy for a product with 2 million requests a month, a hard 400 ms p95 requirement on one endpoint and a quality-critical path on another. Include the deprecation plan."
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Common mistakes

- **Choosing by leaderboard.** General rankings and your narrow task disagree more often than not.
- **Comparing cost per call.** Count prompt overhead, output length, retries and thinking tiles.
- **Picking the best model rather than the cheapest good-enough one.** The difference is margin on every request forever.
- **Hard-coding the model name.** It turns a routine deprecation into a migration project.
- **Skipping the re-evaluation on upgrade.** Newer is not automatically better *for your task*.
